#Here is the problem 2

```{r import-data, message=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

clean_file <- "data/analysis_births_2023_2025.csv.gz"

# Verify the file location.
stopifnot(file.exists(clean_file))

# Read the compressed CSV using base R.
# Explicit column types keep the smoking and outcome indicators logical.
births <- local({
  con <- gzfile(clean_file, open = "rt")
  on.exit(close(con))

  read.csv(
    con,
    colClasses = c(
      year = "integer",
      maternal_age = "integer",
      cigarettes_daily_trimester1 = "integer",
      smoked_trimester1 = "logical",
      birth_weight_g = "integer",
      low_birth_weight = "logical"
    ),
    na.strings = c("", "NA"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})

required_columns <- c(
  "year",
  "maternal_age",
  "cigarettes_daily_trimester1",
  "smoked_trimester1",
  "birth_weight_g",
  "low_birth_weight"
)

# Confirm the required columns and expected number of records.
stopifnot(
  all(required_columns %in% names(births)),
  nrow(births) == 10474625
)

names(births)
nrow(births)
```
```{r weight-distribution, fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
# Check the columns needed for this figure.
stopifnot(
  all(c("birth_weight_g", "smoked_trimester1") %in% names(births)),
  !anyNA(births$birth_weight_g),
  !anyNA(births$smoked_trimester1),
  all(births$birth_weight_g > 0)
)

# Count births within each 100-g interval.
weight_bins <- births |>
  mutate(
    # Example: 3,245 g belongs to the interval [3,200, 3,300).
    bin_start = floor(birth_weight_g / 100) * 100,

    smoking_group = factor(
      smoked_trimester1,
      levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),
      labels = c("No reported smoking", "Reported smoking")
    )
  ) |>
  count(smoking_group, bin_start, name = "births_in_bin") |>
  group_by(smoking_group) |>
  mutate(
    # Each group's percentages sum to 100%.
    percent = 100 * births_in_bin / sum(births_in_bin)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

# Confirm that every record contributed to the figure.
stopifnot(sum(weight_bins$births_in_bin) == nrow(births))

weight_distribution_plot <- ggplot(
  weight_bins,
  aes(x = bin_start + 50, y = percent)
) +
  geom_col(width = 100, fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 2500,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "firebrick",
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ smoking_group, ncol = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Birth-weight distributions by smoking status",
    subtitle = "Reported first-trimester smoking, 2023–2025",
    x = "Birth weight (g)",
    y = "Births within smoking group (%)",
    caption = "Dashed line: 2,500-g low-birth-weight threshold."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

weight_distribution_plot
```
Birth-weight distributions overlapped substantially, but the distribution among births with reported first-trimester smoking was shifted toward lower weights. This group also had a larger proportion of births below the 2,500-g low-birth-weight threshold. Percentages were calculated within each smoking group to account for differences in group size. These descriptive findings motivate examining whether low-birth-weight probability varies across smoking-intensity categories and maternal age groups.

```{r create-analysis-groups}
# Set the category order for tables, models, and plots.
dose_labels <- c("0", "1–4", "5–9", "10–19", "20+")
age_labels <- c(
  "Under 20", "20–24", "25–29", "30–34", "35–39", "40+"
)

# Verify that the required analysis variables are complete.
stopifnot(
  !anyNA(births$maternal_age),
  !anyNA(births$cigarettes_daily_trimester1),
  !anyNA(births$low_birth_weight),
  is.logical(births$low_birth_weight)
)

# Summarize births within each year, age group, and smoking category.
cells <- births |>
  group_by(
    year = factor(year),
    age = cut(
      maternal_age,
      breaks = c(-Inf, 19, 24, 29, 34, 39, Inf),
      labels = age_labels
    ),
    dose = cut(
      cigarettes_daily_trimester1,
      breaks = c(-1, 0, 4, 9, 19, Inf),
      labels = dose_labels
    )
  ) |>
  summarise(
    total = n(),
    low = sum(low_birth_weight),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(other = total - low)

# Confirm that grouping retained every eligible birth.
stopifnot(
  sum(cells$total) == nrow(births),
  !anyNA(cells)
)

# Pool years to create the descriptive age–smoking table.
observed <- cells |>
  group_by(age, dose) |>
  summarise(
    total = sum(total),
    low = sum(low),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(observed_pct = 100 * low / total)
```

```{r smoking-distribution, fig.width=9, fig.height=6}
# Calculate the percentage in each smoking category within each age group.
smoking_distribution <- observed |>
  group_by(age) |>
  mutate(
    age_total = sum(total),
    category_pct = 100 * total / age_total
  ) |>
  ungroup()

# Each panel shows one smoking-intensity category.
# Compare maternal age groups within each panel.
ggplot(
  smoking_distribution,
  aes(x = age, y = category_pct)
) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", width = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ dose, ncol = 3, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Reported smoking intensity by maternal age",
    subtitle = "Panel labels indicate cigarettes per day in the first trimester",
    x = "Maternal age group",
    y = "Eligible births within age group (%)",
    caption = "Vertical scales vary across panels."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```

Most eligible births had no reported first-trimester smoking across all maternal age groups. However, the distribution of smoking intensity differed by age. Reporting 1–4 cigarettes daily was most common among mothers aged 20–24, whereas reporting 10–19 cigarettes daily generally became more common with increasing age. Reporting 20 or more cigarettes daily was least common among mothers under 20 and relatively similar across groups aged 25 and older. These descriptive differences support considering maternal age when examining the association between smoking intensity and low birth weight.





We examined low birth weight, defined as birth weight below 2,500 g, across five categories of reported first-trimester smoking intensity. Model 1 included smoking intensity, maternal age group, and birth year as categorical predictors. Model 2 additionally included an interaction between smoking intensity and maternal age group. We compared the models using a likelihood-ratio test. For interpretation, we averaged Model 2’s predicted probabilities over a common birth-year distribution and calculated percentage-point differences relative to no reported smoking within each age group.

```{r}
# Model 1: Estimate the smoking-intensity association,
# adjusting for maternal age group and birth year.
model1 <- glm(
  cbind(low, other) ~ dose + age + year,
  family = binomial(),
  data = cells
)

# Model 2: Allow the smoking-intensity association to vary by age group.
# update() keeps the same outcome, data, and adjustment variables.
model2 <- update(model1, . ~ . + dose:age)

# Verify that both models converged.
stopifnot(model1$converged, model2$converged)

# Test all smoking-intensity × age interaction terms together.
interaction_test <- anova(model1, model2, test = "Chisq")
interaction_test
```
After adjustment for birth year, the association between reported first-trimester smoking intensity and the odds of low birth weight varied across maternal age groups (likelihood-ratio test for interaction, χ²(20) = 1,387.5, p < 0.001).

#Show how large the differences are

```{r}
# Count eligible births in each year. These counts supply the weights.
year_weights <- cells |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(n_births = sum(total), .groups = "drop")

# Create one row for every age group, smoking category, and year.
prediction_grid <- tidyr::crossing(
  year_weights,
  age = levels(cells$age),
  dose = levels(cells$dose)
)

# Get Model 2's predicted probability of low birth weight for each row.
prediction_grid$prob <- predict(
  model2, newdata = prediction_grid, type = "response"
)

# Average across years, then compare each dose with zero in the same age group.
age_results <- prediction_grid |>
  group_by(age, dose) |>
  summarise(
    adjusted_pct = 100 * weighted.mean(prob, n_births),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  group_by(age) |>
  mutate(difference_pp = adjusted_pct - adjusted_pct[dose == "0"]) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    age = factor(age, levels = levels(cells$age)),
    dose = factor(dose, levels = levels(cells$dose))
  ) |>
  arrange(age, dose)

# Display the same smoking comparison for all six age groups.
age_results |>
  filter(dose == "1–4") |>
  select(age, adjusted_pct, difference_pp) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 2,
    col.names = c("Maternal age", "Adjusted low birth weight at 1–4/day (%)",
                  "Difference from 0/day (percentage points)")
  )

# Display the observed age–smoking summary in the report.
observed |>
  select(age, dose, total, low, observed_pct) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 2,
    format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
    col.names = c(
      "Maternal age",
      "Cigarettes/day",
      "Eligible births",
      "Low-birth-weight births",
      "Observed low birth weight (%)"
    )
  )
```

After standardizing to a common distribution of birth years, the estimated difference in low birth weight between births with reported first-trimester smoking of 1–4 cigarettes/day and births with no reported smoking increased across maternal age groups. The difference was 3.66 percentage points among mothers under 20, 9.11 points among those aged 30–34, and 12.61 points among those aged 40 or older. Across all five smoking categories, the likelihood-ratio test supported an interaction between smoking intensity and maternal age on the log-odds scale (χ²(20) = 1,387.5, p < 0.001).


```{r calculate-adjusted-ci}
# Use the same predictor coding and coefficient order as Model 2.
X <- model.matrix(
  delete.response(terms(model2)),
  data = prediction_grid,
  contrasts.arg = model2$contrasts,
  xlev = model2$xlevels
)

beta <- coef(model2)
V <- vcov(model2)

stopifnot(
  model2$converged,
  all(is.finite(beta)),
  all(is.finite(V))
)

X <- X[, names(beta), drop = FALSE]
V <- V[names(beta), names(beta), drop = FALSE]

# Predict the probability for every age–dose–year combination.
predicted_prob <- plogis(drop(X %*% beta))

combinations <- prediction_grid |>
  distinct(age, dose)

age_results_ci <- bind_rows(
  lapply(seq_len(nrow(combinations)), function(i) {

    # Select the birth-year rows for this age–dose combination.
    rows <- which(
      prediction_grid$age == combinations$age[i] &
      prediction_grid$dose == combinations$dose[i]
    )

    # Apply the same birth-year distribution to every combination.
    w <- prediction_grid$n_births[rows]
    w <- w / sum(w)

    p <- predicted_prob[rows]
    p_standardized <- sum(w * p)

    # Delta-method gradient of the weighted average probability.
    gradient <- colSums(
      sweep(
        X[rows, , drop = FALSE],
        1,
        w * p * (1 - p),
        FUN = "*"
      )
    )

    variance_p <- as.numeric(t(gradient) %*% V %*% gradient)
    se_p <- sqrt(max(variance_p, 0))

    # Construct confidence limits on the logit scale so that
    # the transformed limits remain between zero and one.
    stopifnot(p_standardized > 0, p_standardized < 1)

    se_logit <- se_p /
      (p_standardized * (1 - p_standardized))

    z <- qnorm(0.975)

    tibble(
      age = as.character(combinations$age[i]),
      dose = as.character(combinations$dose[i]),
      adjusted_pct = 100 * p_standardized,
      lower_95 = 100 * plogis(
        qlogis(p_standardized) - z * se_logit
      ),
      upper_95 = 100 * plogis(
        qlogis(p_standardized) + z * se_logit
      )
    )
  })
) |>
  mutate(
    age = factor(age, levels = levels(cells$age)),
    dose = factor(dose, levels = levels(cells$dose))
  ) |>
  arrange(age, dose)
```

```{r}
# Use the new results containing the confidence limits.
ggplot(
  age_results_ci,
  aes(x = dose, y = adjusted_pct, group = 1)
) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = lower_95, ymax = upper_95),
    width = 0.18,
    color = "black",
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ age, ncol = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Low birth weight by smoking intensity and maternal age",
    subtitle = "Year-standardized probabilities with 95% confidence intervals",
    x = "Reported cigarettes per day in the first trimester",
    y = "Year-adjusted probability of low birth weight",
    caption = "Model 2 estimates; black bars show pointwise 95% confidence intervals."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```


After standardizing to a common birth-year distribution, estimated low-birth-weight probabilities were higher in every reported smoking category than in the zero-cigarette category within each maternal age group. However, probabilities did not increase consistently across higher smoking-intensity categories. Confidence intervals were generally wider among smoking groups aged under 20 and 40 or older, indicating greater uncertainty in these estimates. These findings describe associations and should not be interpreted as causal effects.



### Q2 conclusion

Reported first-trimester smoking was associated with a higher estimated
probability of low birth weight in every maternal age group. However,
the estimated probabilities did not increase consistently across
higher smoking-intensity categories.

Adding the smoking-intensity-by-age interaction improved model fit
(likelihood-ratio test:
χ²(`r interaction_test$Df[2]`) =
`r sprintf("%.1f", interaction_test$Deviance[2])`,
p `r if (interaction_test[["Pr(>Chi)"]][2] < 0.001) "< 0.001" else paste0("= ", sprintf("%.3f", interaction_test[["Pr(>Chi)"]][2]))`).
This supports variation in the smoking-intensity association across
maternal age groups on the log-odds scale.

After standardizing to a common birth-year distribution, the estimated
difference between 1–4 and 0 cigarettes/day was
`r sprintf("%.2f", with(age_results, difference_pp[age == "Under 20" & dose == "1–4"]))`
percentage points among mothers under 20 and
`r sprintf("%.2f", with(age_results, difference_pp[age == "40+" & dose == "1–4"]))`
percentage points among mothers aged 40 or older.

The confidence intervals describe uncertainty around individual adjusted
probabilities. They do not directly test differences between smoking
categories.

### Limitations

These findings describe associations and do not establish causation.
The models accounted for maternal age group and birth year, but other
factors could explain part of the observed differences. Reported smoking
may be misclassified, and excluding births with missing smoking or
birth-weight information could affect the results. Confidence intervals
do not account for these potential sources of bias.
